title: Belonging remains widespread but local cohesion slips as financial stress, housing, isolation, and unequal safety sort social connection
source_unit: Helen Clark Foundation, Social Cohesion in New Zealand 2026
geography: New Zealand; population-weighted 2025 survey of adults, with Māori, Pacific, and Asian booster samples

observations.period: 2025; national and local belonging, trust, and isolation

denominator.unit: New Zealand adults surveyed in November-December 2025; population-weighted estimates

national_belonging.unit: percent feeling a sense of belonging to New Zealand

local_community_strong.unit: percent feeling a strong sense of community in their local area

government_trust.unit: percent trusting the government to do the right thing

young_isolation.unit: approximately percent of under-30s feeling isolated at least sometimes

cohesion_gradient.value: National belonging remains high while local belonging, institutional trust, and everyday connection are weaker

observations.method: Annual national social-cohesion survey modeled on the Scanlon Foundation Social Cohesion Monitor, with population weighting and booster samples for Māori, Pacific, and Asian communities.
observations.uncertainty: The report is a repeated cross-sectional survey; belonging and isolation are self-reported and do not establish causal direction between trust, local connection, and material conditions.
observations.subgroup: New Zealand adults, under-30s, Māori, Pacific, Asian, and other population groups.
observations.counterinterpretation: High national belonging may reflect a broad symbolic identity that does not require strong local participation or government trust.

denominator.unit: New Zealand adults in the population-weighted social-cohesion survey

food_insecurity.unit: approximately percent sometimes going without meals because food is unaffordable

young_food_insecurity.unit: approximately percent of under-30s sometimes going without meals because of cost

financial_stress_prediction.value: Financial stress predicts low belonging, low trust, high isolation, and more negative attitudes to immigration more strongly than most measured variables

belonging_buffer.value: People under financial pressure who retain strong belonging remain involved in their communities at rates similar to financially comfortable people

observations.method: Population-weighted survey associations comparing financial stress, belonging, community involvement, trust, isolation, and immigration attitudes.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not disclose full model specifications, effect sizes, or temporal ordering; belonging may buffer stress, be produced by resources, or reflect common causes.
observations.subgroup: Financially stressed adults, under-30s, and respondents with strong or weak belonging.
observations.counterinterpretation: Community involvement may be differently reported by people with different social norms, and the apparent protective role of belonging may not imply material relief.

observations.period: 2025; housing, cross-cultural friendship, and local civic connection

denominator.unit: New Zealand adults in the population-weighted social-cohesion survey

homeowner_participation_gap.unit: percentage-point higher civic participation among homeowners than renters

homeowner_belonging_gap.unit: percentage-point higher neighbourhood belonging among homeowners than renters

cross_cultural_friendship.unit: percent with at least one close friend from a different ethnic or religious background

friendship_belonging.value: People with close cross-cultural friends consistently report stronger belonging

housing_as_cohesion.value: Housing tenure appears as a social-cohesion condition, not only a financial or shelter condition

observations.method: Survey comparisons of housing tenure, civic participation, neighbourhood belonging, friendship networks, and social connection.
observations.uncertainty: Homeownership is correlated with age, income, stability, neighbourhood duration, and wealth; the reported gaps are not causal tenure effects.
observations.subgroup: Homeowners and renters; respondents with and without cross-cultural or cross-religious friendships.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stable residence or socioeconomic position may generate both homeownership and belonging, while friendship may be an outcome rather than a driver of cohesion.

observations.period: 2025; unequal safety, media habits, and political meaning

denominator.unit: New Zealand adults in the population-weighted social-cohesion survey

women_night_safety.unit: percent of women feeling safe walking alone at night

men_night_safety.unit: percent of men feeling safe walking alone at night

social_media_bad.unit: percent saying social media is bad for society

social_media_frequency.unit: percent using social media several times a day

strong_leader_young.unit: percent of under-30s supporting a strong leader who bypasses Parliament

hope_gap.value: Young people are highly aspirational but report the weakest lived cohesion, creating a gap between imagined and experienced futures

observations.method: Population-weighted survey comparisons across gender, age, social-media use, political attitudes, and perceived safety.
observations.uncertainty: The public page does not provide full question wording, subgroup bases, or causal models for safety, media use, political preference, and cohesion.
observations.subgroup: Women and men, under-30s and over-65s, social-media users, and respondents with different political attitudes.
observations.counterinterpretation: Support for a strong leader may express frustration with institutional performance rather than a settled anti-democratic commitment; safety perceptions may reflect different routines and exposure.

related_sources.claim: Helen Clark Foundation research program context.
Scanlon Foundation Social Cohesion Monitor model referenced as the comparative survey basis.

boundary: This record adds a belonging-and-material-stress route: national belonging can remain high while local cohesion, trust, safety, and hope weaken; financial stress, housing tenure, cross-cultural friendship, age, gender, and media habits sort exposure. It does not establish causal effects, clinical loneliness, actual civic behavior, or policy impact.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Helen Clark Foundation publication page reviewed for survey sample, weighting, belonging, trust, isolation, financial stress, food insecurity, housing, friendship, safety, media, youth, and limitations available in the public summary.
